## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on
the complete usual filtered probability space of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]. Let $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$.
Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius matrix norm. Let $W$ be an adapted
standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are independent of
the current filtration. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel,
and suppose finite nonnegative constants $L,K$ satisfy, for all $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ |b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|, $$
$$ |b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2), $$
and
$$ |b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F \le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}. $$
Let $X_0$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$. Let $X$ be the exact continuous
strong solution with
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^2<\infty, $$
and let $Y^h,\bar Y^h$ be the continuous Euler interpolation and left-endpoint
step process of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. The
uniform pointwise moment and interpolation-increment bounds of
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] then imply that a
constant $C$, independent of $h$, satisfies
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch. $$
Thus the grid-point root-mean-square error is $O(h^{1/2})$. The constant may
depend on $T,d,m,L,K$ and the exact-solution supremum-moment bound supplied by
the P-SDE-01 existence theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; finite $d,m$; the stated horizon, Brownian, coefficient and initial-value hypotheses; the exact strong solution $X$ and its finite supremum second moment; and the Euler recursion/interpolation.

[F1] The continuous Euler interpolation is $Y_t=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)(t-t_k)+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})$ on $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$, with $Y_{t_k}=Y_k$ and left-endpoint step process $\bar Y_t=Y_k$ on $[t_k,t_{k+1})$. [[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]

[F2] Under the stated global Lipschitz, linear-growth, half-Hölder time, Brownian-increment and initial-value conditions, $\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E|\bar Y_t|^2$ and $\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t|^2$ are bounded uniformly in $h$, and $\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^2\le C h$. [[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]]

[F3] For each scalar Brownian integral $M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ with finite energy, $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\mathbb E\int_0^TH_s^2ds$. [[thm-doob-maximal-bound-for-the-ito-integral]]

[F4] For a finite-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process, its component processes have the coordinatewise drift and Brownian-integral representation stated in the definition. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]

[F5] Stopping a finite-energy Brownian Itô integral at a stopping time agrees with integrating its predictable stopped integrand. [[thm-stopping-an-ito-integral]]

[F6] If $v(t)\le A+\int_0^t Bv(s)\,ds$ for nonnegative continuous $v$ and constants $A,B\ge0$, then $v(t)\le Ae^{Bt}$. [[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]

[F7] The stated squared growth bound implies $|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le\sqrt2K(1+|x|)$; with the global Lipschitz, usual-filtration and initial-value conditions, the P-SDE-01 theorem supplies a unique exact strong solution and $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^2<\infty$. [[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]

[F8] A map $\rho$ is a stopping time when $\{\rho\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t\ge0$. [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]

[F9] For a continuous adapted process, the supremum on $[0,t]$ equals the supremum over rational times in $[0,t]$ together with $t$, and is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable. [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]

[F10] Cauchy–Schwarz for time integrals gives $|\int_0^t u_s\,ds|^2\le t\int_0^t|u_s|^2ds$. [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]

[F11] If $Z_R\uparrow Z$ are nonnegative measurable random variables, then $\mathbb E Z_R\uparrow\mathbb E Z$. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[A1] AC is stated because the SDE, Brownian, Itô-integral and maximal-inequality interfaces in [F3]–[F7] adopt it. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]

1.1 By [F4] and [F7], the exact process has its finite-coordinate Itô representation; [F1] supplies the Euler interpolation and its predictable representative $\bar Y^-$ with left-endpoint map $\eta_h^-$. Use that representative in the Euler integral form: $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)ds+\int_0^t\sigma(s,X_s)dW_s,$ $Y_t^h=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y_s^-)ds+\int_0^t\sigma(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y_s^-)dW_s.$ The grid-valued coefficients are predictable on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$; their finite expected energy follows from the uniform pointwise second moments in [F2] and the linear-growth bounds, while the exact coefficients have finite energy by the stated $\mathbb E\sup|X|^2$ bound and the same growth condition. Thus these are the required integral representations. In subsequent estimates, $\bar Y$ and $\eta_h$ may replace their predictable versions because they differ only at finitely many grid times, which do not affect the integrals. For $R>0$ define $\tau_R=\inf\{t\le T:|e_t|\ge R\}\wedge T$, with $\inf\emptyset=\infty$. For $t<T$, $\{\tau_R\le t\}=\{\sup_{s\le t}|e_s|\ge R\}$, which is in $\mathcal F_t$ by continuity and [F9]; for $t\ge T$ the event is all of $\Omega$. Thus [F8] makes $\tau_R$ a stopping time. Subtracting the displays and using [F5] gives the stopped error as the sum of the two stopped coefficient integrals. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F7, F8, F9, given]

1.2 Put $\delta b_s=b(s,X_s)-b(\eta_h(s),\bar Y_s),\qquad \delta\sigma_s=\sigma(s,X_s)-\sigma(\eta_h(s),\bar Y_s).$ The state Lipschitz bounds, time modulus, and $|X_s-\bar Y_s|\le|e_s|+|Y_s^h-\bar Y_s|$ give $|\delta b_s|^2+\|\delta\sigma_s\|_F^2 \le C\left(|e_s|^2+|Y_s^h-\bar Y_s|^2+h(1+|\bar Y_s|^2)\right).$ Consequently, with $v_R(t)=\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|e_{s\wedge\tau_R}|^2$, [F2] bounds the expected drift-integrand error and the expected squared diffusion-integrand error, after stopping, by $C\int_0^t v_R(s)ds+Ch.$ [F1, F2, F10, given, algebra]

2.1 Cauchy–Schwarz for time integrals bounds the squared supremum of the stopped drift integral by $T\int_0^t\mathbb E[1_{\{s\le\tau_R\}}|\delta b_s|^2]ds$. For the vector stochastic integral, write each state coordinate as a sum of the $m$ scalar Brownian integrals and use $|\sum_{j=1}^m z_j|^2\le m\sum_j|z_j|^2$. Applying [F3] to each scalar term yields the bound $4m\mathbb E\int_0^t1_{\{s\le\tau_R\}}\|\delta\sigma_s\|_F^2ds$. Using step 1.2 in both bounds gives $v_R(t)\le C\int_0^t v_R(s)ds+Ch,$ where $C$ is independent of $R$ and $h$. [F2, F3, F10, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The stopped error is bounded by $R$, so $v_R$ is finite and continuous; applying [F6] to step 2.1 gives $v_R(T)\le C_T h$ uniformly in $R$. Since $e$ is continuous on the compact interval, $\tau_R=T$ for all sufficiently large $R$ on each sample path. Taking $R=n\in\mathbb N$, the stopped suprema increase to $\sup_{s\le T}|e_s|^2$; monotone convergence [F11] yields $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|e_t|^2\le C_T h$. Taking square roots gives the grid-point root-mean-square rate. AC enters only through [A1], and no arbitrary-index choice is used in the estimates. [A1, F6, F11, step 2.1, given] ∎

## Remarks

The proof is the finite-$L^2$ interpolation-defect route. It uses the
pointwise-in-time moment and increment estimates of the scheme supplier; its
stopping argument does not assume a path-supremum moment bound for the Euler
interpolation. This rate is proved separately from the autonomous
Higham–Mao–Stuart all-moment theorem.

3.1 The stopped error is bounded by $R$, so $v_R$ is finite and continuous; applying [F6] to step 2.1 gives $v_R(T)\le C_T h$ uniformly in $R$. pointwise-in-time moment and increment estimates of the scheme supplier; its
stopping argument does not assume a path-supremum moment bound for the Euler
interpolation. This rate is proved separately from the autonomous
Higham–Mao–Stuart all-moment theorem.

    - title: "Simo Särkkä and Arno Solin, Applied Stochastic Differential Equations, §8.1"
      url: "https://users.aalto.fi/~asolin/sde-book/sde-book.pdf"

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, and fix $T>0$. Work on a
complete filtered probability space whose filtration is right-continuous and
contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in $\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be
an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments after
time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Let $X_0$ be finite and
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, and independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$. Use the Euclidean state norm and Frobenius
matrix norm. Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be autonomous $C^1$ coefficients.
Assume finite constants $\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for
all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ \langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2,\qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2, $$
$$ |f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2. $$
For each $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h$ a positive integer, let $Y^h$ be the
continuous Euler–Maruyama interpolation and $\bar Y^h$ its left-endpoint step
process from [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]], using this same $W$ and $X_0$.
Assume that for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$ \sup_{0<h\le1,\ T/h\in\mathbb N} \left(\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t^h|^p+ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|\bar Y_t^h|^p\right)<\infty. $$
Then for every even integer $r\ge2$ there is a finite constant $C_r$, independent
of $h$, such that
$$ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t^h-\bar Y_t^h|^r\le C_r h^{r/2}. $$
The premise is an all-moment premise for this autonomous coefficient class; it
does not follow from the finite-$L^2$ moment bound alone.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; finite dimensions $d,m$; $T>0$; the stated complete right-continuous filtered space, adapted Brownian motion and initial value; the $C^1$, one-sided-Lipschitz, diffusion-Lipschitz and polynomial drift inequalities in the Statement; $0<h\le1$ with $T/h\in\mathbb N$; and the uniform all-moment bounds stated there.

[F1] On $[t_k,t_{k+1}]$, the continuous Euler interpolation is
$Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})$, while $\bar Y_t=Y_k$ on
$[t_k,t_{k+1})$ and $Y_T=\bar Y_T=Y_N$.
[[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]]

[F2] If a Brownian coordinate has increment law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then for every integer $n\ge1$ its $2n$th absolute moment is $(2n-1)!!|t-s|^n<\infty$.
[[lem-gaussian-even-moment-bound-for-brownian-increments]]

[F3] A standard finite-dimensional Brownian motion has independent coordinates, each a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion; its vector increments have law $N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$.
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]

[A1] AC is declared because the deterministic Brownian-increment and Gaussian-moment interfaces used in [F2] and [F3] assume it. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof


1.1 Fix $t\in[t_k,t_{k+1})$ and put $r_t=Y_t^h-\bar Y_t^h$ and $\delta=t-t_k$. By [F1], $r_t=\delta f(Y_k^h)+g(Y_k^h)(W_t-W_{t_k}).$ For even $r\ge2$, the finite-dimensional power inequality gives $|r_t|^r\le2^{r-1}\left(\delta^r|f(Y_k^h)|^r+ \|g(Y_k^h)\|_F^r|W_t-W_{t_k}|^r\right).$ [F1, algebra]

2.1 Taking $y=0$ in the coefficient bounds gives $|f(x)|^2\le2|f(0)|^2+2D(1+|x|^q)|x|^2, \qquad \|g(x)\|_F^2\le2\|g(0)\|_F^2+2c|x|^2.$ Thus $|f(x)|^r\le C_r(1+|x|^{(q+2)r/2})$ and $\|g(x)\|_F^r\le C_r(1+|x|^r)$. The uniform all-moment premise therefore bounds both coefficient moments in step 1.1 uniformly over $h$ and $t$. [given, algebra]

2.2 Each coordinate of $W_t-W_{t_k}$ has the Gaussian law in [F3], so [F2] and the finite-dimensional inequality $|z|^r\le C_{r,m}\sum_{j=1}^m|z_j|^r$ give $\mathbb E|W_t-W_{t_k}|^r\le C_{r,m}\delta^{r/2}$. Since $Y_k^h$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and Brownian increments are independent of $\mathcal F_{t_k}$, conditioning in step 1.1 separates the coefficient factor from this Gaussian moment. [F2, F3, given]

3.1 Using $0\le\delta\le h\le1$, so $\delta^r\le\delta^{r/2}$, steps 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2 yield $\mathbb E|Y_t^h-\bar Y_t^h|^r\le C_r h^{r/2}$ uniformly for $t<T$. At grid points the increment is zero by [F1], including $t=T$. The constants depend on $r,T,d,m,c,D,q,f(0),g(0)$ and the stated moment bounds, but not on $h$. AC is inherited only through [A1] and the declared Gaussian interfaces; no arbitrary-index choice is used in the estimate. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎
## Source notes

Higham–Mao–Stuart, Lemma 4.3, proves this interpolation increment estimate
under its autonomous one-sided-Lipschitz and all-moment hypotheses. The proof
above records the growth and Gaussian-moment steps needed here explicitly.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ |b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|, $$
$$ |b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2), $$
and
$$ |b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}. $$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

## Remarks

This algorithm defines finite-dimensional recursions. Its definition alone
does not assert a convergence rate, density regularity, or a path-supremum
moment bound.

## Statement

Assume AC. Fix $T>0$ and a finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$.
Let $W$ be a scalar Brownian motion adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)$, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N(0,t-s)$ for
every $0\le s<t\le T$. If each $\xi_k$ is real-valued,
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and square-integrable, then the predictable
step process
$$H_s=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\xi_k1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s)$$
is square-integrable. The continuous version of its Itô integral is
indistinguishable on $[0,T]$ from
$$S_t=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\xi_k\bigl(W_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-W_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The coefficients need not be bounded.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $T>0$, a finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$, a scalar Brownian motion adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)$ whose every future increment is independent of the current filtration, and square-integrable $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients $\xi_k$.

[F1] [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]: increments over a positive time interval have the corresponding centered normal law.

[F12] [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]: Brownian paths are continuous on one common measurable event of probability one.

[F2] [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]: the predictable sigma-algebra is generated by time-zero sets and rectangles $(s,t]\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$; a process is predictable when its time-sample map is measurable for that sigma-algebra.

## Definition

Use the data and grid of [[alg-euler-maruyama]], and let
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ be its recursion. The left-endpoint map is
$$ \eta_h(t)=\max\{t_k:t_k\le t\},\qquad 0\le t\le T. $$
The right-continuous step process is
$$ \bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N. $$
The continuous interpolation is the pathwise process
$$ Y_t=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)(t-t_k)+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}). $$
At a shared grid endpoint the formulas agree because the recursion gives
$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k})$.
In particular $Y_{t_k}=Y_k$ for every $k$, including $Y_T=Y_N$.

For stochastic integration, define the predictable left-endpoint version by
$\bar Y^-_0=Y_0$ and $\bar Y^-_s=Y_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, and set
$\eta_h^-(0)=0$ and $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$. Its coefficient
integrands use the same fixed left endpoints. When the recursion is adapted,
each coordinate of $\bar Y^-$ and each coefficient composition is a
predictable finite-step process: on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ its value is
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable. These coefficients need not be bounded, so the
integrands need not be elementary in the bounded-coefficient sense of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Values at the finitely many
grid points do not change either integral. Once square integrability is
established, [[lem-square-integrable-predictable-step-ito-integral-is-finite-sum]]
identifies each finite-coordinate Itô integral of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] with its
finite-sum version, giving the equivalent formula
$$ Y_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,ds+\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t \sigma_{\cdot j}(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,dW_s^j. $$
where $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ and
$\sigma_{\cdot j}$ denotes column $j$ of the matrix.

The justified-by theorem
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] establishes the
required integrability and well-definedness under the stated coefficient and
initial-moment conditions.

## Remarks

The distinction between $\bar Y$ and $\bar Y^-$ is only at deterministic
grid times. The first records the value used at each time by the left-endpoint
convention; the second is the predictable representative used by the
stochastic integral.

## Example

Let $\Theta=Y=\{0,1\}$, give each parameter prior probability $1/2$, and set $K(\theta,\{y\})=3/4$ when $y=\theta$ and $1/4$ otherwise. On the canonical joint space $\Omega=\Theta\times Y$, the posterior RCD is the random probability measure $L(\omega,\cdot)=\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$, where $\Pi_y(y)=3/4$ and $\Pi_y(1-y)=1/4$. The RCD is evaluated at a sample point $\omega$; the data-indexed version is the separate kernel $y\mapsto\Pi_y$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite model and the canonical joint probability specified in the example.

[F1] A proper Bayesian model supplies a prior probability and a parameter-measurable sampling probability kernel. [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]

[F2] A posterior RCD is indexed by the sample point, while a data-indexed posterior is a kernel on the data space whose composition with $Y$ satisfies the conditional-law identity. [[def-bayesian-posterior-as-regular-conditional-law]]

[F3] The prior and sampling kernel define the joint probability on the product space. [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]

## Verification

## Definition

Let a proper Bayesian model be given, and let $J$ be its joint prior-predictive probability on $(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$, supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. More generally, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X:\Omega\to\Theta$ and $Y:\Omega\to\mathsf Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). A **posterior regular conditional distribution (posterior RCD)** is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, in the sense of [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. It is a kernel indexed by the sample point $\omega\in\Omega$. The canonical realization is $\Omega=\Theta\times\mathsf Y$ with $Q=J$ and coordinate maps $X(\theta,y)=\theta$, $Y(\theta,y)=y$.

A **data-indexed posterior kernel** is a probability kernel $\Pi_{\cdot}$ from $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ to $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) for which $\omega\mapsto\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ ([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). Equivalently, for every $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$Q(X\in A,\ Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,Q_Y(dy),$$
where $Q_Y$ is the data marginal (equal to $J_Y$). This kernel is indexed by data values, not sample points.

The definition asserts no existence of either conditional kernel. Values of a data-indexed version on a measurable $J_Y$-null set are not fixed by the conditional-law identities; replacing them there by a fixed probability preserves those identities. A dominated-density construction is a separate route: [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] requires a proper prior, a sigma-finite data measure, and a specified jointly measurable sampling density, and fills fibres whose marginal density is zero or infinite with the prior. It does not require the data space to be standard Borel.

## Example

Work on a complete filtered probability space whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains all $P$-null subsets of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be an adapted standard one-dimensional Brownian motion
whose increments after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$. For
$dX_t=-X_t\,dt+dW_t$, $X_0=0$, and $T=1$, couple the Euler paths with
fine step $h=1/(2n)$ and coarse step $2h=1/n$ by summing each pair of fine
Brownian increments for the coarse update. For $\varphi(x)=\cos x$, the
shared-Brownian theorem gives correction variance $O(h)$, strong bias
$O(h^{1/2})$, and coupled path work $O(h^{-1})$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the complete usual filtered Brownian setup above on $[0,1]$; the $\mathcal F_0$-measurable initial value $X_0=0$; $h=1/(2n)$ for $n\ge1$; the fine/coarse coupling described in the Example; and $\varphi(x)=\cos x$.

[F1] Under the stated nested-grid coupling and a globally Lipschitz payoff, the Euler correction has second moment $O(h)$, its variance is $O(h)$, the strong-route bias is $O(h^{1/2})$, and fixed-refinement path work is $O(h^{-1})$. [[thm-shared-brownian-euler-level-correction-rates]]

[F2] For a real continuous Brownian Itô process $X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_sds+\int_0^t\sigma_sdW_s$, applying Itô's formula to $e^tX_t$ is valid and gives the displayed drift and diffusion terms. [[thm-ito-formula-one-dimensional]]

[F3] For a square-integrable Brownian Itô integral $M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dW_s$, $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\mathbb E\int_0^TH_s^2ds$. [[thm-doob-maximal-bound-for-the-ito-integral]]

[F4] A standard Brownian motion has independent normal increments of variance equal to the elapsed time. [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]

[A1] The refinement factor is $M=2$; each coarse increment is the sum of its two fine increments, and both paths start from the same $X_0$ and use the same Brownian path.

[A2] The payoff is globally Lipschitz with constant $1$, since $|\cos x-\cos y|=|\int_y^x-\sin s\,ds|\le|x-y|$.

[A3] AC is inherited through the Brownian and Itô interfaces in [F2]–[F4]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Verification


1.1 The coefficients are $b(x)=-x$ and $\sigma(x)=1$. They are globally Lipschitz with constant $1$, satisfy $|b(x)|^2+|\sigma(x)|^2=x^2+1$, and are time independent, so the shared coefficient and time-modulus conditions hold. Applying [F2] to $e^tX_t$ gives $X_t=e^{-t}\int_0^t e^s dW_s$. Applying [F2] to $e^tW_t$ then gives $X_t=\int_0^t e^{-(t-s)}dW_s =W_t-\int_0^t e^{-(t-s)}W_sds.$ Hence $\sup_{t\le1}|X_t|\le2\sup_{t\le1}|W_t|$, and [F3] gives $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le1}|X_t|^2\le16<\infty$. [A3, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 The payoff satisfies [A2]. The fine and coarse meshes obey $h\le1/2$, $1/h=2n\in\mathbb N$, and $1/(2h)=n\in\mathbb N$; [A1] makes every coarse increment the corresponding Brownian increment over its full interval, and [F4] verifies its filtration-relative law and independence. Thus the shared-rate theorem hypotheses hold. [A1, A2, F4, given]

2.1 Applying [F1] yields $\operatorname{Var}(\cos(Y_1^h)-\cos(Y_1^{2h}))\le Ch, \qquad |\mathbb E\cos(X_1)-\mathbb E\cos(Y_1^h)|\le C\sqrt h,$ and work $O(h^{-1})$ per coupled path pair. These rates correspond to $(\alpha,\beta)=(1/2,1)$ for this payoff. [F1, step 1.2] ∎

## Example

Let $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ with prior $\Pi(1)=1/3$, and let $Y=\{0,1,2\}$ have its power-set sigma-algebra. Given $\theta=1$, assign probabilities $(1/4,3/4,0)$ to $(0,1,2)$; given $\theta=0$, assign probabilities $(3/4,1/4,0)$. The posterior probability of $\theta=1$ is $1/7$ after data $0$ and $3/5$ after data $1$. Data value $2$ has prior-predictive probability zero, so two versions may assign different posterior laws there.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite parameter and data spaces and the prior and sampling probabilities specified in the example.

[F1] A proper Bayesian model consists of a prior probability and a parameter-measurable sampling probability kernel. [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]

[F2] A data-indexed posterior kernel satisfies the rectangle conditional-law identity; its values on prior-predictive null data may vary by version. [[def-bayesian-posterior-as-regular-conditional-law]]

[F3] A proper prior and sampling kernel define the joint law by $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\Pi(d\theta)$. [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]

## Verification

**Given:** The assumptions and finite model in the example.

1.1 The joint masses are $J(1,0)=1/12$, $J(0,0)=1/2$, $J(1,1)=1/4$, and $J(0,1)=1/6$, while both masses at data $2$ are zero. Therefore $J_Y(0)=7/12$, $J_Y(1)=5/12$, and $J_Y(2)=0$. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Define $\Pi_0(1)=1/7$, $\Pi_1(1)=3/5$, and choose any probability law for $\Pi_2$; set $\Pi_y(0)=1-\Pi_y(1)$. Each $\Pi_y$ is a probability, and measurability is automatic on the finite power-set data space. The displayed ratios give $\Pi_0(1)J_Y(0)=J(1,0)$ and $\Pi_1(1)J_Y(1)=J(1,1)$; subtraction from the marginal gives the same identities for parameter value $0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 For any $A\subseteq\Theta$ and $B\subseteq Y$, summing the singleton identities in step 2.1 over $y\in B$ gives $\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,J_Y(dy)=J(A\times B)$; the zero-mass term at $y=2$ contributes zero for every choice of $\Pi_2$. Thus every such kernel is a data-indexed posterior version by [F2]. In particular, $\Pi_2=\delta_0$ and $\widetilde\Pi_2=\delta_1$, with the same values at $0,1$, are distinct versions of the same posterior law. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ with prior $\Pi(1)=1/3$, and let $Y=\{0,1,2\}$ have its power-set sigma-algebra. [F3] A proper prior and sampling kernel define the joint law by $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\Pi(d\theta)$. [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]

## Example

Let the data set be a disjoint union $\mathsf Y=U\sqcup V\sqcup W$ of three uncountable sets, with sigma-algebra consisting of all unions of these three atoms and reference probability $\nu(U)=\nu(V)=\nu(W)=1/3$. This measurable space is not standard Borel: distinct points of $U$ cannot be separated by a measurable set, whereas every standard-Borel space separates distinct points. **Given:** The measurable data space, reference probability $\nu$, finite parameter space, prior, and sampling densities specified in the example.

[F2] The posterior is a conditional law; a data-indexed posterior version must satisfy the rectangle identity. [[def-bayesian-posterior-as-regular-conditional-law]]

[F3] A proper prior and a sampling kernel with a specified jointly measurable density against a sigma-finite data measure have the displayed posterior kernel on fibres where the marginal density is finite and positive. [F4] A standard-Borel space is measurably isomorphic to a Polish space. [[def-standard-borel-space]]

[F5] In a Polish space the topology is induced by a metric, so singleton sets are closed and Borel. [[def-polish-space]]

[F6] The product sigma-algebra contains measurable rectangles; on the finite parameter space, simple functions constant on such rectangles are jointly measurable. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

**Given:** The assumptions and finite model in the example.

Assigning mass $1/3$ to each disjoint atom defines a probability measure $\nu$: a pairwise disjoint family has at most three nonempty members, so countable additivity reduces to finite additivity on the atoms. ---

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

## Sources

Van Handel's Chapter 5.1 specifies the integral-equation interpretation and
finite-horizon filtered setup. Van der Vaart's Section 7.1 treats strong
solutions on a given filtered space and indistinguishability. The local
definition fixes the vector/matrix coordinate convention and the exact
coefficient and initial-value assumptions used by the following proofs.

$N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for a fixed finite

## Example

Work on a complete filtered probability space whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains all $P$-null subsets of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be an adapted standard one-dimensional Brownian motion
whose increments after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$. On
$[0,1]$, solve the additive-noise Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation
$$ dX_t=-X_t\,dt+dW_t,\qquad X_0=0. $$
For $h=1/N\le1/2$, couple the Euler recursion to the same Brownian path. The
finite-$L^2$ theorem gives the general strong supremum bound
$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le1}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2=O(h)$; in this additive-noise example the
terminal root-mean-square error is in fact $O(h)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the complete usual filtered Brownian setup above; $T=1$; the $\mathcal F_0$-measurable initial value $X_0=0$; $h=1/N\le1/2$; and the SDE and Euler recursion displayed in the Example.

[F1] The Euler recursion is $Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k$, and the continuous interpolation agrees with the recursion at grid points. [[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]

[F2] For a one-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process and $F\in C^{1,2}$, Itô's formula has drift $F_t+bF_x+\frac12\sigma^2F_{xx}$ and stochastic term $\sigma F_x\,dW$. [[thm-ito-formula-one-dimensional]]

[F3] For a deterministic finite-energy integrand $q$, $\mathbb E(\int_0^Tq_s\,dW_s)^2=\int_0^Tq_s^2ds$. [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]]

[F4] For a deterministic step integrand, its Itô integral is the corresponding finite sum of Brownian increments. [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]

[F5] Under global state-Lipschitz, linear-growth, half-Hölder time, and square-integrable initial-value assumptions, the Euler strong supremum error satisfies $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch$. [[thm-euler-maruyama-strong-rate-for-square-integrable-initial-data]]

[A1] AC is included because the Brownian, Itô-formula and Itô-integral suppliers in [F2]–[F4] assume it. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Example

Work on a complete filtered probability space whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains all $P$-null subsets of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be an adapted standard one-dimensional Brownian motion
whose increments after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Compare the
target equation $dX_t=dW_t$, $X_0=0$, on $[0,1]$ with a learned
equation $d\widehat X_t=(\pi/2)dt+dW_t$, $\widehat X_0=0$. For the bounded
Lipschitz payoff $\varphi(x)=\cos x$, the Euler solver is exact at the
terminal grid point for the learned equation, while the learned drift creates
a nonzero bias relative to the target law that is independent of $h$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the complete usual filtered Brownian setup above; $T=1$; the $\mathcal F_0$-measurable initial values $X_0=\widehat X_0=0$; $h=1/N$; the target and learned equations in the Example; and $\varphi(x)=\cos x$.

[F1] A one-dimensional standard Brownian motion has $W_1\sim N(0,1)$. [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]

[F2] If $Z\sim N(m,v)$, its characteristic function is $\mathbb E e^{itZ}=\exp(imt-vt^2/2)$. [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-normal-law]]

[F3] The Euler–Maruyama recursion uses $Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k$. [[alg-euler-maruyama]]

[F4] Under global Lipschitz, linear-growth, half-Hölder time and square-integrable initial-value hypotheses, the Euler strong supremum error tends to zero at root-mean-square rate $O(h^{1/2})$. [[thm-euler-maruyama-strong-rate-for-square-integrable-initial-data]]

[A1] AC is stated because the Brownian and normal characteristic-function interfaces in [F1]–[F2] assume it. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Verification


1.1 The target equation has terminal value $X_1=W_1$. By [F1]–[F2], $\mathbb E\cos(X_1)=\operatorname{Re}\mathbb E e^{iW_1}=e^{-1/2}.$ The learned Euler recursion is $\widehat Y_{k+1}=\widehat Y_k+(\pi/2)h+\Delta W_k$. Summing its $N$ increments gives $\widehat Y_N=\frac\pi2 Nh+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Delta W_k=\frac\pi2+W_1,$ which is exactly $\widehat X_1$ for every $h=1/N$. 2.1 By [F2] and the addition formula, $\mathbb E\cos(\widehat X_1) =\operatorname{Re}\left(e^{i\pi/2}\mathbb E e^{iW_1}\right)=0.$ Therefore the absolute expectation bias relative to the target is $|0-e^{-1/2}|=e^{-1/2}>0$ for every step size, so it persists as $h\to0$. The solver theorem [F4] controls error to the learned SDE solution; it supplies no bound on the difference between the learned and target drifts. AC is inherited through [A1]. [A1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $\Theta=\{0,1\}$ have prior probabilities $1/2,1/2$, and let the data space be $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ with its power-set sigma-algebra. For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, set $f_0(n)=2^{-(n+1)}$ and $f_1(n)=\frac23(\frac13)^n$. These are two geometric sampling laws. The prior-predictive mass is $m(n)=\frac12(f_0(n)+f_1(n))>0$, and a data-indexed posterior is
$$\Pi_n(1)=\frac{f_1(n)}{f_0(n)+f_1(n)},\qquad \Pi_n(0)=\frac{f_0(n)}{f_0(n)+f_1(n)}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the finite parameter space, prior, and countable data model in the example.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice (AC), as required by the general standard-Borel RCD route. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The prior probability and sampling kernel define the proper Bayesian model. [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]

[F2] A data-indexed posterior kernel is a probability kernel whose composition with the observation is a posterior RCD. [[def-bayesian-posterior-as-regular-conditional-law]]

[F3] When both the parameter and data spaces are standard Borel, the posterior RCD factors through the data coordinate as a measurable posterior kernel. [[thm-standard-borel-bayesian-posterior-kernel-exists]]

[F4] For $0\le r<1$, the geometric series satisfies $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n=(1-r)^{-1}$. [[thm-geometric-series]]

[F5] A standard-Borel space is measurably isomorphic to a Polish space. [[def-standard-borel-space]]

[F6] A Polish space is a separable space whose topology is induced by a complete metric. [[def-polish-space]]

## Verification

**Given:** The assumptions and countable model in the example.

1.1 The discrete metric on $\mathbb N_0$ is complete because every Cauchy sequence is eventually constant; $\mathbb N_0$ itself is a countable dense subset. Its topology is discrete, so its Borel sigma-algebra is the power set. The finite discrete parameter space has the same properties. Thus both spaces are standard Borel by [F5]–[F6]. By [F4], $\sum_nf_0(n)=1$ and $\sum_nf_1(n)=1$, so they define probability sampling laws and the prior in [F1] gives a Bayesian model. [given, F1, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 Since both spaces are standard Borel and AC holds, [F3] supplies a data-indexed posterior kernel. For every $n$, both $f_0(n)$ and $f_1(n)$ are positive and finite, so $m(n)>0$ and the displayed values are in $[0,1]$ and sum to one. Every function on the discrete data space is measurable, hence $n\mapsto\Pi_n$ is a probability kernel. [given, A1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $i\in\{0,1\}$ and every $B\subseteq\mathbb N_0$, $\sum_{n\in B}\Pi_n(i)m(n)=\frac12\sum_{n\in B}f_i(n)=J(\{i\}\times B)$. Adding the identities for $i=0,1$ proves the rectangle identity for every $A\subseteq\Theta$ and every data event $B$. Thus the explicit kernel is a data-indexed posterior version; all its data values have positive prior-predictive mass. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let a proper Bayesian model have joint prior-predictive law $J$, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X,Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). If $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ is standard Borel ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), then a posterior RCD of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$ exists. The data space $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ need only be measurable. In particular, the claim applies to the canonical product realization supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A proper Bayesian model with prior-predictive joint law $J$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$, and random elements $X,Y$ on it with joint law $J$. Assume AC and that $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ is standard Borel.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice (AC). [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A proper prior probability and a parameter-measurable sampling probability kernel define a joint probability $J$ on the product, with $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\Pi(d\theta)$. [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]

[F2] A random element is a measurable map and its law is the pushforward probability on its target. [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]

[F3] A random element into a standard-Borel target has a regular conditional distribution given any sub-sigma-algebra, under AC. [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]]

[F4] A posterior RCD is an RCD of the parameter coordinate $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$ on this canonical joint probability space. [[def-bayesian-posterior-as-regular-conditional-law]]

## Proof

**Given:** The model, measurable spaces, and hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 By [F1], the model's prior and sampling kernel define the joint probability $J$ on the canonical product space. The given random elements $X,Y$ have this same joint law, and [F2] supplies the random-element and pushforward-law meanings used for this realization. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 The target $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ is standard Borel and AC is assumed. Apply [F3] to $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$, the given random element $X$, and the sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G=\sigma(Y)$. It gives an RCD of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$; by [F4] this is the stated posterior RCD. The RCD theorem places no standard-Borel condition on $\mathsf Y$. [given, A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, choose] ∎

## Statement

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the complete usual filtered Brownian space, $T\ge0$, finite
$d,m\ge1$, jointly Borel coefficients with the stated uniform global
Lipschitz and linear-growth constants, an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable
$X_0\in L^2$ independent of future Brownian increments, and the Axiom of
Choice as required by the Itô-integral interfaces.

[F1] The Picard map $\Phi$ is well-defined on adapted continuous inputs with
finite $L^2$ path supremum; it has the path-sup difference estimate with
$C_d=2TL^2+8mL^2$, the growth estimate with
$C_T=6K^2T+24mK^2$, and the first-iterate bound
$(4K^2T^2+16mK^2T)(1+E|X_0|^2)$. [[lem-lipschitz-sde-map-is-well-defined]]

[F2] A strong solution is an adapted continuous process on the given space
with the locally defined finite-coordinate Itô integral equation satisfied
indistinguishably. The complete filtration contains all null sets at time zero.
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]

[F3] The declared Itô-integral and martingale interfaces use the Axiom of
Choice; the Picard recursion, integer bounds, and stopping conventions below
make no further selections. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F4] Cauchy–Schwarz bounds expectations by second moments; monotone
convergence passes to expectations of nonnegative partial sums, and Fatou
passes the finite-tail $L^2$ bounds to their pointwise limit.
[[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] [[thm-fatou-lemma]]

[F5] For a continuous path, its supremum on $[0,T]$ equals the supremum over
rational times in $[0,T]$ and the endpoint $T$. [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]

[F6] Every adapted continuous solution of the same SDE with the stated
initial-value and coefficient hypotheses has finite $E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t|^2$.
[[lem-lipschitz-sde-local-solution-has-finite-path-moment]]

[F7] Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges. Hence, on each path
where the Picard iterates are uniformly Cauchy, their finitely many coordinate
sequences have real limits; these limits form the pointwise $\mathbb R^d$
limit, and the uniform Cauchy bound passes to that limit.
[[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]

## Proof

1.1 If $T=0$, set $X_0$ as the sole value of the process; both integrals vanish, the path-sup bound follows from $(1+3E|X_0|^2)\ge E|X_0|^2$, and any two solutions with that initial value agree. For $T>0$, let $\Phi$ be the map of [F1], set $X^0_t=X_0$, and recursively set $X^{n+1}=\Phi(X^n)$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Put $a_n(t)=E\sup_{u\le t}|X^n_u-X^{n-1}_u|^2$ for $n\ge1$. By [F1], $a_1(T)\le A_T:= (4K^2T^2+16mK^2T)(1+E|X_0|^2)$ and $a_{n+1}(t)\le C_d\int_0^t a_n(s)ds$. Induction on $n$ gives $a_n(t)\le A_TC_d^{n-1}t^{n-1}/(n-1)!$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The majorant series $\sum_{n\ge1}\sqrt{A_TC_d^{n-1}T^{n-1}/(n-1)!}$ converges. If $A_T=0$, it is identically zero; if $C_dT=0$, every term after the first is zero; otherwise the ratio of consecutive terms is $\sqrt{C_dT/n}\to0$. By [F4], $E\sup|X^n-X^{n-1}|\le\sqrt{a_n(T)}$ and monotone convergence gives $E\sum_n\sup|X^n-X^{n-1}|=\sum_nE\sup|X^n-X^{n-1}|<\infty$; hence that nonnegative series is finite almost surely. On this event, for every $t$ the vector sequence $(X^n_t)_n$ is Cauchy, since $\sup_{u\le T}|X^m_u-X^n_u|\le\sum_{j=n+1}^m\sup_{u\le T}|X^j_u-X^{j-1}_u|$; [F7] gives the coordinate limits and therefore a vector limit $X_t$. Letting $m\to\infty$ in the same inequality bounds $\sup_{t\le T}|X^n_t-X_t|$ by the tail of the summable series, which tends to zero. Thus the convergence is almost surely uniform. For finite tails the $L^2$ triangle inequality follows by expanding the square and applying Cauchy–Schwarz, so $\|X^m-X^n\|_{L^2(\sup)}\le\sum_{j=n+1}^m\sqrt{a_j(T)}$. Fatou's lemma [F4] then gives $E\sup_{t\le T}|X^n_t-X_t|^2\le(\sum_{j=n+1}^{\infty}\sqrt{a_j(T)})^2\to0$. [F4, F7, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 Let $A$ be the measurable probability-one event on which that series of path suprema is finite; measurability follows because each supremum is a supremum over the countable dense set in [F5]. Uniform convergence makes $X$ continuous on $A$; completeness gives $A^c\in\mathcal F_0$, so set $X_t=X_0$ on $A^c$. For each fixed $t$, the limit on $A$ of the $\mathcal F_t$-measurable $X^n_t$, together with the $\mathcal F_0$-measurable value on $A^c$, is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable. Thus $X$ is adapted and continuous, and its $L^2$ path-sup convergence places it in the class of [F2]. [F2, F5, step 3.1, given]

5.1 For every $n$, $X^{n+1}=\Phi(X^n)$. The difference estimate of [F1] gives $E\sup_{u\le T}|\Phi(X^n)_u-\Phi(X)_u|^2\le C_dT E\sup_{u\le T}|X^n_u-X_u|^2\to0$. Since $X^{n+1}\to X$ in the same norm by step 3.1, uniqueness of an $L^2$ limit implies $\Phi(X)=X$ indistinguishably. Hence $X$ satisfies the SDE. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Write $f(t)=E\sup_{u\le t}|X_u|^2$. The growth estimate of [F1] and $X=\Phi(X)$ imply $f(t)\le3E|X_0|^2+C_T\int_0^t(1+f(s))ds$. Put $g=1+f$ and $H(t)=1+3E|X_0|^2+C_T\int_0^tg(s)ds$. Then $g\le H$, $H(0)=1+3E|X_0|^2$, and $H'(t)=C_Tg(t)\le C_TH(t)$ almost everywhere. Consequently $(e^{-C_Tt}H(t))'\le0$ almost everywhere, so $f(T)\le g(T)\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT}$. [F1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 If $Y$ is any other strong solution with the same data, then $Y=\Phi(Y)$ by [F2] and $Y\in\mathcal H_T$ by [F6]. The difference estimate in [F1] gives $q(t):=E\sup_{u\le t}|X_u-Y_u|^2\le C_d\int_0^tq(s)ds$. With $Q(t)=C_d\int_0^tq(s)ds$, one has $Q(0)=0$ and $Q'\le C_dQ$ almost everywhere, hence $Q=q=0$. Thus $\sup_{t\le T}|X_t-Y_t|=0$ almost surely, which is indistinguishability. AC is exactly the inherited assumption [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, F6, step 5.1] ∎

## Remarks

The proof uses no ellipticity or nondegeneracy of $\sigma$. The result gives
strong existence, uniqueness, and moment control only; it implies no
transition-density regularity, forward Kolmogorov uniqueness, or reversal
theorem.

## Sources

Van Handel, Chapter 5.1, Theorems 5.1.3 and 5.1.5 with proofs, and van der
Vaart, Section 7.1, Theorem 7.8 with proof, independently develop Picard
iteration and Gronwall uniqueness. The proof here supplies the vector
coordinate estimates, complete path-space limit argument, and exact
finite-horizon supremum bound under the displayed hypotheses.

## Statement

Use the coefficient and initial-value hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on a finite horizon $[0,T]$. If $Y$ is
any adapted continuous solution of that SDE whose drift and diffusion
integrals are locally defined as in the Definition, then
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|Y_t|^2<\infty.$$
Thus the usual local-integrability definition of strong solution entails the
path-sup square-integrability used by the Picard estimates.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** a finite horizon $T\ge0$, the usual filtered Brownian space,
jointly Borel coefficients with global Lipschitz constant $L$ and linear-growth
constant $K$, an $\mathcal F_0$ initial value $X_0\in L^2$, and an adapted
continuous solution $Y$ satisfying the SDE integral identity.

[F1] A strong solution has adapted continuous paths, the stated initial value,
and locally defined drift and finite-coordinate Itô integrals. The resulting
process belongs to the continuous Brownian Itô-process class when its drift
variation and diffusion energy are finite almost surely.
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]

[F2] Adapted continuous processes are predictable and progressive; the
multidimensional Itô formula applies to continuous Brownian Itô processes and
$C^{1,2}$ functions. Tonelli's theorem permits the expected time-integral
interchanges below for the nonnegative measurable coefficient and stopped
integrands. [[lem-adapted-continuous-processes-are-progressively-measurable]] [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F3] For a stopping time, stopping an Itô integral is the same as integrating
against $1_{[0,\tau]}H$; a finite-energy integral is a mean-zero
square-integrable martingale and has the scalar Itô maximal bound.
[[thm-stopping-an-ito-integral]] [[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]] [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]] [[thm-doob-maximal-bound-for-the-ito-integral]]

[F4] The first-hitting time of a continuous adapted path can be checked by
measurability of its supremum over rational times and the endpoint.
[[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]

[F5] Fatou's lemma passes a pointwise almost-sure limit of nonnegative
variables to the lower bound on their expectations. [[thm-fatou-lemma]]

[F6] The Itô-integral and Itô-formula suppliers use Full AC, already included
in the SDE data convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 If $T=0$, $Y_0=X_0$ and the claim is $E|X_0|^2<\infty$. Suppose $T>0$. 2.1 The multidimensional Itô formula [F2] for $U(x)=1+|x|^2$, stopped at $\tau_R$, has drift $2Y_s\cdot b(s,Y_s)+\|\sigma(s,Y_s)\|_F^2$ and martingale integrand $2Y_s^{\mathsf T}\sigma(s,Y_s)$. 3.1 Set $H_R(t)=E(1+|X_0|^2)+C_0\int_0^tg_R(s)ds$. Then $g_R\le H_R$ and $H_R'\le C_0H_R$ almost everywhere, so $(e^{-C_0t}H_R(t))'\le0$. Therefore $g_R(t)\le E(1+|X_0|^2)e^{C_0t}$. [step 2.1, algebra]

## Sources

moment control. This lemma supplies the exact implication needed for

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on a complete filtered
probability space whose filtration is right-continuous and contains every
$P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in $\mathcal F_0$. Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$
be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are
independent of the current filtration. Let
$X_0$ be finite and $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$. Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius
matrix norm. Consider
the autonomous SDE
$$ X_t=X_0+\int_0^t f(X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t g(X_s)\,dW_s, \qquad X_t\in\mathbb R^d, $$
where $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ are $C^1$. Assume that constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ \langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2, \qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2, $$
and
$$ |f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2. $$
For each $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, let $Y^h$ be the continuous
Euler–Maruyama interpolation and $\bar Y^h$ its left-endpoint step process
from [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]]. Assume
that an exact strong solution $X$ and these exact, step and continuous Euler
processes have uniformly bounded moments of every finite order on $[0,T]$:
for every $p\ge1$,
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^p+ \sup_{0<h\le1,\ T/h\in\mathbb N}\left( \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t^h|^p+ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|\bar Y_t^h|^p\right)<\infty. $$
Then a constant $C$, independent of $h$, satisfies
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch. $$
In particular the grid-point root-mean-square error is $O(h^{1/2})$.
The all-moment premise is part of this source contract; $X_0\in L^2$ alone
does not imply it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; finite $d,m$; $T>0$; the stated Brownian and coefficient hypotheses; an exact strong solution $X$; and the uniform all-moment bounds in the Statement.

[F1] The autonomous Euler algorithm returns the grid recursion, left-endpoint step process, and continuous interpolation using $Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})$; endpoint values agree with the recursion. [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]]

[F2] For every even integer $r\ge2$, the autonomous Euler interpolation increment satisfies $\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^r\le C_rh^{r/2}$ under the all-moment and coefficient premises stated in that lemma. [[lem-euler-maruyama-autonomous-interpolation-increment-moments]]

[F3] For a finite-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process and $F\in C^{1,2}$, Itô's formula has drift $\partial_tF+b\cdot\nabla F+\frac12(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}):D^2F$ and stochastic term $\nabla F\,\sigma\,dW$. [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]]

[F4] For a finite-energy $m$-dimensional Brownian Itô integral $N_t=\sum_j\int_0^tK_s^j\,dW_s^j$, $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|N_t|\le16\sqrt m\,\mathbb E(\int_0^T\sum_j|K_s^j|^2ds)^{1/2}$. [[lem-brownian-ito-integral-l1-maximal-bound]]

[F5] If $U,V\in L^2$, then $\mathbb E|UV|\le(\mathbb E U^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E V^2)^{1/2}$. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

[F6] If $v(t)\le A+\int_0^t Bv(s)\,ds$ for nonnegative continuous $v$ and constants $A,B\ge0$, then $v(t)\le Ae^{Bt}$. [[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]

[F7] A finite-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process is an adapted continuous solution of its coordinatewise drift-plus-Itô-integral equation on the given usual filtered space. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]

[A1] AC is stated because the Brownian, Itô-process, multidimensional Itô and maximal-integral interfaces in [F3], [F4], and [F7] adopt it. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof



**Given:** AC; finite $d,m$; $T>0$; the stated Brownian and coefficient hypotheses; an exact strong solution $X$; and the uniform all-moment bounds in the Statement.

[F1] The autonomous Euler algorithm returns the grid recursion, left-endpoint step process, and continuous interpolation using $Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})$; endpoint values agree with the recursion. [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]]

[F2] For every even integer $r\ge2$, the autonomous Euler interpolation increment satisfies $\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^r\le C_rh^{r/2}$ under the all-moment and coefficient premises stated in that lemma. [[lem-euler-maruyama-autonomous-interpolation-increment-moments]]

[F3] For a finite-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process and $F\in C^{1,2}$, Itô's formula has drift $\partial_tF+b\cdot\nabla F+\frac12(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}):D^2F$ and stochastic term $\nabla F\,\sigma\,dW$. [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]]

[F4] For a finite-energy $m$-dimensional Brownian Itô integral $N_t=\sum_j\int_0^tK_s^j\,dW_s^j$, $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|N_t|\le16\sqrt m\,\mathbb E(\int_0^T\sum_j|K_s^j|^2ds)^{1/2}$. [[lem-brownian-ito-integral-l1-maximal-bound]]

[F5] If $U,V\in L^2$, then $\mathbb E|UV|\le(\mathbb E U^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E V^2)^{1/2}$. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

[F6] If $v(t)\le A+\int_0^t Bv(s)\,ds$ for nonnegative continuous $v$ and constants $A,B\ge0$, then $v(t)\le Ae^{Bt}$. [[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]

[F7] A finite-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process is an adapted continuous solution of its coordinatewise drift-plus-Itô-integral equation on the given usual filtered space. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]

[A1] AC is stated because the Brownian, Itô-process, multidimensional Itô and maximal-integral interfaces in [F3], [F4], and [F7] adopt it. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]




1.1 Induction in the recursion shows that $Y_k^h$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable: this holds for $Y_0=X_0$, and each update uses $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients and a Brownian increment measurable at $t_{k+1}$. The interpolation is therefore adapted and continuous. For integration use the predictable step representative $\widehat Y_0^h=Y_0$ and $\widehat Y_s^h=Y_k^h$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$; its coefficient processes $f(\widehat Y^h)$ and $g(\widehat Y^h)$ are predictable because each $Y_k^h$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and $f,g$ are continuous. It agrees with $\bar Y^h$ outside the finite set of grid times. The recursion and interpolation give the same integral equation with these predictable coefficients. Setting $y=0$ in the coefficient inequalities yields $|f(x)|^2\le2|f(0)|^2+2D(1+|x|^q)|x|^2$ and $\|g(x)\|_F^2\le2\|g(0)\|_F^2+2c|x|^2$. The all-moment premise thus gives finite expected time-integral energy for these Euler coefficients; it gives the same for $f(X)$ and $g(X)$. The definition [F7] then makes the Euler interpolation and exact solution continuous Brownian Itô processes, and its linear-combination clause makes their difference $e$ one as well. In Itô's formula for $|e_t|^2$, the drift is $2\langle e_t,f(X_t)-f(\widehat Y_t^h)\rangle+\|G_t\|_F^2$ and the martingale term is $M_t=2\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t\langle e_s,G_{s,\cdot j}\rangle\,dW_s^j$, where $G_s=g(X_s)-g(\widehat Y_s^h)$. Since $e$ is continuous adapted and $G$ is predictable, each martingale integrand is predictable. Its finite expected energy follows from $\sum_j|2\langle e_s,G_{s,\cdot j}\rangle|^2\le4|e_s|^2\|G_s\|_F^2$ and $\mathbb E\int_0^T|e_s|^2\|G_s\|_F^2ds\le T(\mathbb E\sup_{s\le T}|e_s|^4)^{1/2}(\mathbb E\sup_{s\le T}\|G_s\|_F^4)^{1/2}<\infty$ by the all-moment and coefficient-growth premises. [F3, F7, given]

1.2 Split the drift difference at $Y_t^h$. The one-sided Lipschitz bound and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ give $2\langle e,f(X)-f(\widehat Y)\rangle \le(2\mu+1)|e|^2+|f(Y)-f(\widehat Y)|^2$ almost everywhere in time. The polynomial local-Lipschitz condition bounds the final term by $D(1+|Y|^q+|\widehat Y|^q)|Y-\widehat Y|^2$. Also, splitting $g(X)-g(\widehat Y)$ at $g(Y)$ and using its global Lipschitz bound gives $\|G\|_F^2\le2c|e|^2+2c|Y-\widehat Y|^2$. By [F2] with $r=2,4$, the all-moment premise, and [F5], $\mathbb E|Y_s-\widehat Y_s|^2\le C h$ and $\mathbb E\big[(1+|Y_s|^q+|\widehat Y_s|^q)|Y_s-\widehat Y_s|^2\big]\le C h$ for almost every $s$, uniformly in $h$. Thus the expected integrated drift is bounded by $C\int_0^t\mathbb E|e_s|^2\,ds+Ch$. [F2, F5, given, algebra]

1.3 Apply [F4] to the vector integrand $K_s^j=2\langle e_s,G_{s,\cdot j}\rangle$. Since $\sum_j|K_s^j|^2\le4|e_s|^2\|G_s\|_F^2$, $\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|M_s| \le32\sqrt m\,\mathbb E\left[\sup_{s\le t}|e_s|\left(\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2ds\right)^{1/2}\right] \le32\sqrt m\left(v(t)\,\mathbb E\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2ds\right)^{1/2},$ where $v(t)=\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|e_s|^2$. From [F2] and the Lipschitz estimate for $g$, $\mathbb E\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds \le C\int_0^t\mathbb E|e_s|^2\,ds+Ch.$ Young's inequality therefore bounds the martingale term by $\frac12v(t)+C\int_0^t v(s)\,ds+Ch$. [F2, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Take the supremum over times up to $t$ in Itô's identity from step 1.1, take expectations, and insert the drift estimate from step 1.2 and martingale estimate from step 1.3. Moving $\frac12v(t)$ to the left gives $v(t)\le C\int_0^t v(s)\,ds+Ch.$ The all-moment assumption makes $v$ finite; pathwise continuity of $e$ and dominated convergence make $v$ continuous. Applying [F6] with the nondecreasing constant term $Ch$ yields $v(T)\le C'h$. The constants depend on $T,d,m,\mu,c,D,q$ and the all-moment bounds, but not on $h$. [F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Since $Y_T^h=Y_N^h$, the grid endpoint is included in the supremum bound. Taking square roots gives the stated root-mean-square order. AC is inherited exactly through [A1]; no choice principle is used in the numerical estimates. [A1, step 2.1] ∎

## Remarks

This is the autonomous all-moment Higham–Mao–Stuart route. It does not replace
the separate finite-$L^2$ theorem, does not extend to nonautonomous
coefficients, and does not derive its all-moment premise from $X_0\in L^2$.
The local proof uses [F4], whose $L^1$ maximal estimate is proved from the

title: "Euler–Maruyama strong rate under Higham–Mao–Stuart hypotheses"

  - def-continuous-brownian-ito-process
  - thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes
  - thm-gronwall-integral-inequality
  - cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables
  - def-axiom-of-choice

  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Desmond J. Higham, Xuerong Mao, and Andrew M. Stuart, Strong Convergence of Euler-Type Methods for Nonlinear Stochastic Differential Equations, §4, Assumptions 3.1/4.1/4.2, Lemma 4.3 and Theorem 4.4"
      url: "https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~dhigham/Publications/P44.pdf"
    - title: "Tiejun Li, Lecture 16: Numerical SDEs: Basics, §2"
      url: "https://www.math.pku.edu.cn/teachers/litj/notes/appl_stoch/lect15.pdf"
    - title: "Simo Särkkä and Arno Solin, Applied Stochastic Differential Equations, §8.1"
      url: "https://users.aalto.fi/~asolin/sde-book/sde-book.pdf"

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on a complete filtered
probability space whose filtration is right-continuous and contains every
$P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in $\mathcal F_0$. Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$
be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are
independent of the current filtration. Let
$X_0$ be finite and $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$. Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius
matrix norm. Consider
the autonomous SDE
$$ X_t=X_0+\int_0^t f(X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t g(X_s)\,dW_s, \qquad X_t\in\mathbb R^d, $$
where $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ are $C^1$. Assume that constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ \langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2, \qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2, $$
and
$$ |f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2. $$
For each $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, let $Y^h$ be the continuous
Euler–Maruyama interpolation and $\bar Y^h$ its left-endpoint step process
from [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]]. Assume
that an exact strong solution $X$ and these exact, step and continuous Euler
processes have uniformly bounded moments of every finite order on $[0,T]$:
for every $p\ge1$,
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^p+ \sup_{0<h\le1,\ T/h\in\mathbb N}\left( \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t^h|^p+ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|\bar Y_t^h|^p\right)<\infty. $$
Then a constant $C$, independent of $h$, satisfies
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch. $$
In particular the grid-point root-mean-square error is $O(h^{1/2})$.
The all-moment premise is part of this source contract; $X_0\in L^2$ alone
does not imply it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; finite $d,m$; $T>0$; the stated Brownian and coefficient hypotheses; an exact strong solution $X$; and the uniform all-moment bounds in the Statement.

[F1] The autonomous Euler algorithm returns the grid recursion, left-endpoint step process, and continuous interpolation using $Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})$; endpoint values agree with the recursion. [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]]

[F2] For every even integer $r\ge2$, the autonomous Euler interpolation increment satisfies $\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^r\le C_rh^{r/2}$ under the all-moment and coefficient premises stated in that lemma. [[lem-euler-maruyama-autonomous-interpolation-increment-moments]]

[F3] For a finite-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process and $F\in C^{1,2}$, Itô's formula has drift $\partial_tF+b\cdot\nabla F+\frac12(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}):D^2F$ and stochastic term $\nabla F\,\sigma\,dW$. [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]]

[F4] For a finite-energy $m$-dimensional Brownian Itô integral $N_t=\sum_j\int_0^tK_s^j\,dW_s^j$, $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|N_t|\le16\sqrt m\,\mathbb E(\int_0^T\sum_j|K_s^j|^2ds)^{1/2}$. [[lem-brownian-ito-integral-l1-maximal-bound]]

[F5] If $U,V\in L^2$, then $\mathbb E|UV|\le(\mathbb E U^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E V^2)^{1/2}$. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

[F6] If $v(t)\le A+\int_0^t Bv(s)\,ds$ for nonnegative continuous $v$ and constants $A,B\ge0$, then $v(t)\le Ae^{Bt}$. [[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]

[F7] A finite-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process is an adapted continuous solution of its coordinatewise drift-plus-Itô-integral equation on the given usual filtered space. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]

[A1] AC is stated because the Brownian, Itô-process, multidimensional Itô and maximal-integral interfaces in [F3], [F4], and [F7] adopt it. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof



**Given:** AC; finite $d,m$; $T>0$; the stated Brownian and coefficient hypotheses; an exact strong solution $X$; and the uniform all-moment bounds in the Statement.

[F1] The autonomous Euler algorithm returns the grid recursion, left-endpoint step process, and continuous interpolation using $Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})$; endpoint values agree with the recursion. [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]]

[F2] For every even integer $r\ge2$, the autonomous Euler interpolation increment satisfies $\sup_{t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^r\le C_rh^{r/2}$ under the all-moment and coefficient premises stated in that lemma. [[lem-euler-maruyama-autonomous-interpolation-increment-moments]]

[F3] For a finite-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process and $F\in C^{1,2}$, Itô's formula has drift $\partial_tF+b\cdot\nabla F+\frac12(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}):D^2F$ and stochastic term $\nabla F\,\sigma\,dW$. [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]]

[F4] For a finite-energy $m$-dimensional Brownian Itô integral $N_t=\sum_j\int_0^tK_s^j\,dW_s^j$, $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|N_t|\le16\sqrt m\,\mathbb E(\int_0^T\sum_j|K_s^j|^2ds)^{1/2}$. [[lem-brownian-ito-integral-l1-maximal-bound]]

[F5] If $U,V\in L^2$, then $\mathbb E|UV|\le(\mathbb E U^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E V^2)^{1/2}$. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]

[F6] If $v(t)\le A+\int_0^t Bv(s)\,ds$ for nonnegative continuous $v$ and constants $A,B\ge0$, then $v(t)\le Ae^{Bt}$. [[thm-gronwall-integral-inequality]]

[F7] A finite-dimensional continuous Brownian Itô process is an adapted continuous solution of its coordinatewise drift-plus-Itô-integral equation on the given usual filtered space. [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]

[A1] AC is stated because the Brownian, Itô-process, multidimensional Itô and maximal-integral interfaces in [F3], [F4], and [F7] adopt it. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]




1.1 Induction in the recursion shows that $Y_k^h$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable: this holds for $Y_0=X_0$, and each update uses $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients and a Brownian increment measurable at $t_{k+1}$. The interpolation is therefore adapted and continuous. For integration use the predictable step representative $\widehat Y_0^h=Y_0$ and $\widehat Y_s^h=Y_k^h$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$; its coefficient processes $f(\widehat Y^h)$ and $g(\widehat Y^h)$ are predictable because each $Y_k^h$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and $f,g$ are continuous. It agrees with $\bar Y^h$ outside the finite set of grid times. The recursion and interpolation give the same integral equation with these predictable coefficients. Setting $y=0$ in the coefficient inequalities yields $|f(x)|^2\le2|f(0)|^2+2D(1+|x|^q)|x|^2$ and $\|g(x)\|_F^2\le2\|g(0)\|_F^2+2c|x|^2$. The all-moment premise thus gives finite expected time-integral energy for these Euler coefficients; it gives the same for $f(X)$ and $g(X)$. The definition [F7] then makes the Euler interpolation and exact solution continuous Brownian Itô processes, and its linear-combination clause makes their difference $e$ one as well. In Itô's formula for $|e_t|^2$, the drift is $2\langle e_t,f(X_t)-f(\widehat Y_t^h)\rangle+\|G_t\|_F^2$ and the martingale term is $M_t=2\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t\langle e_s,G_{s,\cdot j}\rangle\,dW_s^j$, where $G_s=g(X_s)-g(\widehat Y_s^h)$. Since $e$ is continuous adapted and $G$ is predictable, each martingale integrand is predictable. Its finite expected energy follows from $\sum_j|2\langle e_s,G_{s,\cdot j}\rangle|^2\le4|e_s|^2\|G_s\|_F^2$ and $\mathbb E\int_0^T|e_s|^2\|G_s\|_F^2ds\le T(\mathbb E\sup_{s\le T}|e_s|^4)^{1/2}(\mathbb E\sup_{s\le T}\|G_s\|_F^4)^{1/2}<\infty$ by the all-moment and coefficient-growth premises. [F1, F3, F7, given]

1.2 Split the drift difference at $Y_t^h$. The one-sided Lipschitz bound and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ give $2\langle e,f(X)-f(\widehat Y)\rangle \le(2\mu+1)|e|^2+|f(Y)-f(\widehat Y)|^2$ almost everywhere in time. The polynomial local-Lipschitz condition bounds the final term by $D(1+|Y|^q+|\widehat Y|^q)|Y-\widehat Y|^2$. Also, splitting $g(X)-g(\widehat Y)$ at $g(Y)$ and using its global Lipschitz bound gives $\|G\|_F^2\le2c|e|^2+2c|Y-\widehat Y|^2$. By [F2] with $r=2,4$, the all-moment premise, and [F5], $\mathbb E|Y_s-\widehat Y_s|^2\le C h$ and $\mathbb E\big[(1+|Y_s|^q+|\widehat Y_s|^q)|Y_s-\widehat Y_s|^2\big]\le C h$ for almost every $s$, uniformly in $h$. Thus the expected integrated drift is bounded by $C\int_0^t\mathbb E|e_s|^2\,ds+Ch$. [F2, F5, given, algebra]

1.3 Apply [F4] to the vector integrand $K_s^j=2\langle e_s,G_{s,\cdot j}\rangle$. Since $\sum_j|K_s^j|^2\le4|e_s|^2\|G_s\|_F^2$, $\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|M_s| \le32\sqrt m\,\mathbb E\left[\sup_{s\le t}|e_s|\left(\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2ds\right)^{1/2}\right] \le32\sqrt m\left(v(t)\,\mathbb E\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2ds\right)^{1/2},$ where $v(t)=\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|e_s|^2$. From [F2] and the Lipschitz estimate for $g$, $\mathbb E\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds \le C\int_0^t\mathbb E|e_s|^2\,ds+Ch.$ Young's inequality therefore bounds the martingale term by $\frac12v(t)+C\int_0^t v(s)\,ds+Ch$. [F2, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Take the supremum over times up to $t$ in Itô's identity from step 1.1, take expectations, and insert the drift estimate from step 1.2 and martingale estimate from step 1.3. Moving $\frac12v(t)$ to the left gives $v(t)\le C\int_0^t v(s)\,ds+Ch.$ The all-moment assumption makes $v$ finite; pathwise continuity of $e$ and dominated convergence make $v$ continuous. Applying [F6] with the nondecreasing constant term $Ch$ yields $v(T)\le C'h$. The constants depend on $T,d,m,\mu,c,D,q$ and the all-moment bounds, but not on $h$. [F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Since $Y_T^h=Y_N^h$, the grid endpoint is included in the supremum bound. Taking square roots gives the stated root-mean-square order. AC is inherited exactly through [A1]; no choice principle is used in the numerical estimates. [A1, step 2.1] ∎

## Remarks

This is the autonomous all-moment Higham–Mao–Stuart route. It does not replace
the separate finite-$L^2$ theorem, does not extend to nonautonomous
coefficients, and does not derive its all-moment premise from $X_0\in L^2$.
The local proof uses [F4], whose $L^1$ maximal estimate is proved from the
published $L^2$ Doob inequality and stopping identity; no unproved
Burkholder–Davis–Gundy supplier is imported.

## Definition

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

## Statement

Assume the SDE data of [[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] and the
global strong solution supplied by
[[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]. For every real
$p\ge2$ with $E|X_0|^p<\infty$, the unique solution satisfies
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}E|X_t|^p\le 2^{p/2}(1+E|X_0|^p)e^{C_pT},\qquad C_p:=\sqrt2\,pK+p(p-1)K^2.$$
The supremum is over the individual-time moments; for $p>2$ this statement
does not assert an $E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^p$ bound. In particular, if $X_0$
has every finite moment of order $p\ge2$, then the solution has uniform
finite-horizon moments of every such order.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the usual filtered-space SDE data, $T\ge0$, $d,m\ge1$, global
Lipschitz and linear-growth coefficients with constant $K$, $X_0\in L^p$
for a fixed real $p\ge2$, and the unique strong solution $X$.

[F1] The unique solution has continuous adapted paths and
$E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^2<\infty$. [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]

[F2] An adapted continuous process is predictable and progressive. Once its
finite-coordinate drift and diffusion coefficients have the local
integrability required by the continuous Brownian Itô-process definition, the
multidimensional $C^{1,2}$ Itô formula holds up to indistinguishability.
Tonelli's theorem justifies the expected time-integral interchanges below for
the nonnegative coefficient and stopped-energy integrands.
[[lem-adapted-continuous-processes-are-progressively-measurable]] [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]] [[thm-multidimensional-ito-formula-for-brownian-driven-processes]] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F3] For a stopping time $\tau$, the stopped integral satisfies
$(H\cdot W)_{t\wedge\tau}=\int_0^t1_{[0,\tau]}H\,dW$; a finite-energy
Itô integral is a square-integrable mean-zero martingale and obeys its
isometry. [[thm-stopping-an-ito-integral]] [[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]] [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]]

[F4] A stopping time is characterized by
$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t$; for a continuous adapted path its supremum
on $[0,t]$ equals the supremum on rational times together with the endpoint.
[[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]

[F5] Fatou's lemma passes a pointwise almost-sure limit of nonnegative
variables to the lower bound on their expectations. [[thm-fatou-lemma]]

[F6] The scalar Itô integral and multidimensional Itô formula carry the
Axiom of Choice; no additional choice is made here. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 If $T=0$, then $|X_0|^p\le2^{p/2}(1+|X_0|^p)$ and the result follows. For $T>0$, put $V(x)=(1+|x|^2)^{p/2}$. It is $C^2$ and $\partial_iV=p x_i(1+|x|^2)^{p/2-1},\quad \partial_{ij}V=p\delta_{ij}(1+|x|^2)^{p/2-1}+p(p-2)x_ix_j(1+|x|^2)^{p/2-2}.$ The gradient bound follows from $|x|\le(1+|x|^2)^{1/2}$. The Hessian is a nonnegative multiple of $I$ plus a nonnegative multiple of $xx^{\mathsf T}$, so it is positive semidefinite. Its eigenvalues orthogonal to $x$ are $p(1+|x|^2)^{p/2-1}$, and the eigenvalue in the $x$ direction is $p(1+|x|^2)^{p/2-2}(1+(p-1)|x|^2)$; each is at most $p(p-1)(1+|x|^2)^{p/2-1}$ because $p\ge2$. At $x=0$ all eigenvalues equal $p$, which obeys the same bound. [given, algebra]

1.2 By [F1], $E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^2<\infty$, so [F2] makes $b(\cdot,X_\cdot)$ progressive and $\sigma(\cdot,X_\cdot)$ predictable. The growth bound gives $E\int_0^T\bigl(|b(s,X_s)|^2+\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2\bigr)ds\le2K^2T(1+E\sup_{s\le T}|X_s|^2)<\infty.$ Thus the drift-square integral and diffusion energy are finite almost surely; pathwise Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds\le\sqrt T(\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|^2ds)^{1/2}<\infty$. Hence $X$ satisfies the continuous Brownian Itô-process hypotheses in [F2]. [F1, F2, given]

1.3 For $R>0$ define $\tau_R:=\inf\{s\in[0,T]:|X_s|\ge R\}\wedge T$, with $\inf\emptyset=+\infty$. For $t<T$, $\{\tau_R\le t\}=\{\sup_{s\le t}|X_s|\ge R\}$; by continuity and [F4] that supremum is measurable using the countable rational times in $[0,t]$ and $t$, all of which are $\mathcal F_t$-measurable. For $t\ge T$ the event is all of $\Omega$, so $\tau_R$ is a stopping time. On $[0,\tau_R]$ the process is bounded by $R$ unless $|X_0|\ge R$, in which case $\tau_R=0$. Hence $1_{[0,\tau_R]}\nabla V(X_s)^{\mathsf T}\sigma(s,X_s)$ is predictable and has finite energy on $[0,T]$. [F1, F2, F4, given]

2.1 Let $\mathcal L_sV(x)=b(s,x)\cdot\nabla V(x)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}(s,x)D^2V(x))$. The inequality $1+|x|\le\sqrt{2(1+|x|^2)}$ follows by squaring and using $(|x|-1)^2\ge0$, so the drift term has absolute value at most $\sqrt2\,pK V(x)$. For each diffusion column $\sigma_{\cdot k}$, positive semidefiniteness and the operator-norm bound give $0\le\sigma_{\cdot k}^{\mathsf T}D^2V\,\sigma_{\cdot k}\le\|D^2V\|_{op}|\sigma_{\cdot k}|^2$.
